newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Crunch week ahead for Burundi leader and Tutsis.
newsitem.headline: Crunch week ahead for Burundi leader and Tutsis.

text.p: The moment of truth is approaching fast for Burundi's military leader, Major Pierre Buyoya, and the Tutsi minority he must defend.

The next week will show whether Buyoya is able, or indeed willing, to take the radical steps demanded by the outside world without losing the backing of an ethnic group which equates concessions to the Hutu majority with suicide.

Ten weeks after the army seized power and put Buyoya in charge, the issues are clear: will he enter serious talks with armed Hutu factions aimed at real power-sharing with Burundi's majority ethnic group?
And if he does, can he remain in office while many Tutsis believe Burundi's Hutus are preparing the same genocide their ethnic brothers committed in neighbouring Rwanda in 1994?

Some of the answers may emerge at a regional summit, slated for October 12. The African leaders who showed rare unity by clamping a total trade embargo on Burundi last July 31 will review policy and decide if Buyoya has done enough to warrant an easing of crippling sanctions.
"The Hutus are no longer willing to negotiate for peanuts. Is Buyoya ready and able to negotiate the substance?" asked a senior European diplomat in Bujumbura.

First, Buyoya needs to receive and accept an invitation to the summit. The array of special envoys flocking to Bujumbura, from the United States, the United Nations and the European Union, want him to be invited.
Buyoya believes that by unbanning political parties, restoring parliament and agreeing in principle to meet Hutu rebels, he has done enough to ease sanctions.
But diplomats say hardliners among pro-sanctions countries, led by Tanzania, are unwilling to relax their grip until the moves to power-sharing are irreversible.
Western governments have dithered on the edges of Burundi's crisis, withholding full endorsement for African sanctions but failing to offer a meaningful alternative.
Now they favour an easing of sanctions.
"The embargo is too tough. Buyoya has almost no room for manoeuvre between the Tutsi hardliners who refuse compromise and the regional leaders demanding it.
"If he gets nowhere at the summit, he will be in very bad shape at home," said one diplomat.
Times have changed since Buyoya stepped down as president in 1993 having lost to a Hutu in Burundi's first fair poll.

Perhaps 150,000 lives have been lost in the past three years of ethnic massacres. They include a president, an archbishop, one-third of the mainstream Hutu party's members of parliament and foreign aid workers.
A Hutu rebellion based in eastern Zaire has grown, nurtured by the failure of peaceful change and the destructive regional rivalries which could rip the heart of Africa apart.
With most of Burundi's interior a no-go zone, estimates vary about the strength of the rebels, led by Leonard Nyangoma's Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD).
Foreign diplomatic analysts agree about one thing: the overwhelmingly Tutsi army cannot wipe out the insurgency.

But nor will the army disintegrate. Young Tutsis are joining up and trades union leaders were unfazed when Buyoya told them on Saturday that far from raising salaries he might ask workers to contribute money to the war effort.
Burundi says the sanctions cost it more than $130 million in the first two months. Worst-hit are the workers and residents of Bujumbura, an eerie town described by one diplomat as a Tutsi fortress.

Despite the privations, ordinary Tutsis show little sign of submission. The danger is in fact "radicalisation", Buyoya's term for the scenario that haunts what is left of Burundi's political centre: a second putsch by army hawks opposed to any dialogue or compromise.
"The embargo is better than death," said Anicet Niyongabo, a trades union leader who is a Tutsi.
"Workers are not willing to accept suicidal measures in order to get the embargo lifted," he said.
A handshake at the next summit with Nyangoma could spell the end for Buyoya, who reshuffled military command and staff jobs in mid-September to strengthen his position.
The army's senior spokesman, Lieutenant-Colonel Longin Minani, does not use language which suggests a political compromise with the rebels is on the agenda.
"This is not a guerrilla war. It is an attempted genocide," he told Reuters.
